summary: This note is a Wikipedia excerpt on the history of Castle Clinton, the fort formerly known as West Battery in New York City. It covers its 1815 renaming after Mayor DeWitt Clinton, its use by the Army, a canceled 1816 office-building proposal amid public opposition, and its transfer to the city in 1822 after the Army stopped using it in 1821.
one_line: History of Castle Clinton, the former West Battery in New York City, from its 1815 renaming to its 1822 transfer to the city.
key_facts: By 1815, West Battery was renamed Castle Clinton, its current official name.
Castle Clinton was named in honor of New York City Mayor DeWitt Clinton.
DeWitt Clinton eventually became Governor of New York.
The castle was converted to administrative headquarters for the Army.
At the end of the war, there was a public movement to build a park in the Battery area.
A 1816 proposal to construct two small office buildings at Castle Clinton was canceled due to public opposition.
Castle Clinton lay dormant for three years after the 1816 proposal was canceled.
In 1820, Castle Clinton was only being used as a paymaster's quarters and storage area.
The United States Army stopped using the fort in 1821.
Castle Clinton was ceded to the city by an act of Congress in March 1822.
By 1822, the bridge leading to Castle Clinton was frequently used by fishermen.
The fishermen were catching fish from the bridge leading to Castle Clinton.
